brief.topic: A six-month bus-priority-lane pilot on Riverton's 6.2 km corridor
brief.desiredChange: Authorize the $6.8 million six-month pilot with reviews at weeks 4, 12, and 24

slides.title: A controlled pilot, with three chances to review
slides.purpose: State the recommended council action and frame the decision as a six-month test with scheduled oversight.
evidence: The proposed bus-priority-lane pilot lasts six months.
Review gates are scheduled at weeks 4, 12, and 24.
slides.focalArtifact: A concise recommendation anchored by the six-month duration and the three review weeks

slides.title: The decision standard
slides.purpose: Define the decision questions the council will use to weigh need, expected effects, trade-offs, cost, and oversight.
evidence: The supplied record covers rider scale, current bus performance, expected bus and car effects, emergency response, cost, duration, and review gates.
slides.focalArtifact: Four decision questions derived from the supplied evidence categories

slides.title: One corridor, 18,400 weekday riders
slides.purpose: Establish the physical scope and the number of weekday bus riders directly exposed to corridor performance.
evidence: The corridor is 6.2 km long.
The corridor carries 18,400 weekday bus riders.

slides.title: The peak bus trip is 34 minutes—and unpredictable
slides.purpose: Show that the current problem includes both peak travel time and substantial variability.
evidence: The peak bus trip is 34 minutes.
Trip variability is plus or minus 9 minutes.
slides.focalArtifact: A 34-minute trip paired with the quoted plus-or-minus 9-minute variability

slides.title: Most delay occurs at intersections
slides.purpose: Identify where the supplied evidence locates the dominant share of corridor delay without adding an unsupported engineering prescription.
evidence: Fifty-eight percent of delay occurs at intersections.

slides.title: The expected bus trip: 34 minutes to 26
slides.purpose: Translate the expected 8-minute reduction into an easy-to-evaluate before-and-expected comparison.
evidence: The current peak bus trip is 34 minutes.
The pilot is expected to reduce the bus trip by 8 minutes.
Twenty-six minutes is the arithmetic result and must be labeled as expected, not observed.
slides.focalArtifact: A current 34-minute trip compared with an expected 26-minute trip

slides.title: The trade-off: three minutes for the typical car trip
slides.purpose: Make the expected road-user trade-off explicit and compare it with the expected bus-time gain.
evidence: The typical car trip is expected to increase by 3 minutes.
The bus trip is expected to decrease by 8 minutes.
slides.focalArtifact: The expected 8-minute bus gain beside the expected 3-minute typical car penalty

slides.title: Emergency response is expected to remain unchanged
slides.purpose: Address the emergency-response constraint directly and faithfully.
evidence: Emergency response is expected to remain unchanged.

slides.title: The six-month test costs $6.8 million
slides.purpose: State the fiscal commitment without inventing unit costs, funding sources, or payback claims.
evidence: The pilot costs $6.8 million.
The pilot lasts six months.

slides.title: The case, on one page
slides.purpose: Synthesize the supplied case for and against authorization so the council can see the whole decision balance.
evidence: There are 18,400 weekday bus riders on the corridor.
The bus trip is expected to decrease by 8 minutes.
The typical car trip is expected to increase by 3 minutes.
Emergency response is expected to remain unchanged.
The pilot costs $6.8 million.
slides.focalArtifact: A single synthesis of rider scale, expected travel-time effects, emergency response, and cost

slides.title: What the forecast does not decide
slides.purpose: Separate proposal expectations from observed pilot results and prevent the council from treating forecasts as completed evidence.
evidence: The 8-minute bus reduction and 3-minute typical car increase are expected outcomes.
Emergency response is expected to remain unchanged.
No additional measurements or outcome thresholds were supplied.
slides.focalArtifact: A boundary between supplied expectations and outcomes that remain to be observed

slides.title: Six months turns a forecast into a decision record
slides.purpose: Explain why the proposal is structured as a time-bounded test rather than a permanent conclusion.
evidence: The proposed pilot lasts six months.
The final supplied review gate is at week 24.
slides.focalArtifact: The six-month pilot period ending in the week-24 review

slides.title: Three review gates keep the council in control
slides.purpose: Sequence the formal review points without inventing numerical pass or fail thresholds.
evidence: Reviews occur at weeks 4, 12, and 24.
slides.focalArtifact: The ordered week-4, week-12, and week-24 review sequence

slides.title: The choice: test the proposal or retain the status quo
slides.purpose: Put the recommended pilot authorization against the alternative of not conducting the test.
evidence: The corridor serves 18,400 weekday bus riders over 6.2 km.
The current peak bus trip is 34 minutes with plus or minus 9 minutes variability.
The expected effects are an 8-minute bus reduction, a 3-minute increase to the typical car trip, and unchanged emergency response.
The six-month pilot costs $6.8 million and has review gates at weeks 4, 12, and 24.
slides.focalArtifact: A binary council choice grounded in the complete supplied decision record

slides.title: Authorize the six-month pilot
slides.purpose: End with a direct motion that incorporates the supplied cost, duration, and oversight schedule.
evidence: The requested authorization is $6.8 million for a six-month pilot.
Reviews are scheduled at weeks 4, 12, and 24.
slides.focalArtifact: The proposed motion to authorize the pilot with all three review gates
